summary:
Lagos State stands under the national framework of Nigeria. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 does not stop at marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Sexual orientation carries exposure before arrival. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states as criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Those religious provisions are recorded for the northern states, not for Lagos.

Entry-level warnings are explicit. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, tells LGBT+ travellers to expect arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, warns of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex unions under the 2014 Act, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia criminal law in some northern states. The arrest, violence and imprisonment warnings apply in Lagos.

Trans identity is not named in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face lethal violence and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found along a highway in Abuja; she had posted about being transgender and working as a sex worker and had expressed fears for her life the previous year. Police stated that preliminary investigations revealed the individual was a man fully dressed in female clothing. Six months later, the Dial (February 2025) records that no suspects had been charged. The evidence is nationally reported and applies in Lagos, with no state-specific divergence recorded.

Enforcement in Lagos has included violence and extortion. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the Act as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, who served a six-month sentence for naira abuse in a maximum-security prison in Lagos. Press coverage at her sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than narrowing it. The scope of the statute, reaching cohabitation, public affection and organisational activity, means an arrest can rest on conduct that carries no independent offence in most comparable jurisdictions.

Official framing of trans victims is a recurring pattern. Police characterised the deceased Abuja Area Mama as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and press coverage of the Bobrisky sentence debated in openly gendered terms which prison should hold her. Both point to documentation risk for a visitor whose证件 or presentation conflicts with the sex recorded by Nigerian authorities.

Proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public add a layer of turbulence around gender expression that sits outside the text of the 2014 Act, and the sources do not establish whether any such proposal has been enacted.

The two documented enforcement episodes in Lagos, the March 2025 beating and extortion of a man for looking gay, and the app-based kito entrapment operations, indicate that risk attaches to perceived identity and to online contact, not only to provable same-sex conduct.

Lagos State police conduct recorded in March 2025 involved striking a man with a gun butt and demanding a 50,000 naira bribe for looking gay, with release coming only after partial payment. Extortion of this kind is a documented feature of encounters in the state.

Bobrisky pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but held that the placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Northern residents under Sharia provisions face exposure that does not apply in Lagos: male sodomy carries the death penalty under state Zina provisions in all twelve northern states, according to the UK Home Office note.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted remains unresolved; the sources available record the proposals and the fear they generated, not their legislative outcome.

No state-specific divergence from the national framework is recorded for Lagos in these sources, and no Lagos statute offering protection on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation is sourced here. The absence of such a statute is not independently verified beyond the national-level findings.

The outcome of the Abuja Area Mama investigation after the February 2025 reporting, including whether any suspect was ever charged, is not sourced.

Placement policy for trans detainees in Nigerian prisons following the October 2024 panel finding is not documented in these sources; the panel addressed the security level of the facility, and no subsequent rule governing male or female section assignment is recorded.

The 2026 travel advice is quoted through Sahara Reporters rather than from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office text itself, so its exact wording and subsequent revision history are unverified here.
